utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Good morning to the technical booth, to the interpreters, to the legal assistants and court reporters, Madam Registrar, Mr. Harmon and Mr. Cayley. Good morning, Mr. Petrusic and Mr. Visnjic, and good morning, Mr. Krstic. Good morning, Witness. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hear you very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are now going to read the solemn declaration that the usher is going to hand you, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may be seated. Are you sitting comfortably?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. You are now going to be shown a piece of paper by the usher, and please say yes or no if it is your name on the piece of paper.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You are now going to be answering questions put to you by Mr. Cayley, who is the gentleman on your right. Mr. Cayley, your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, learned Defence counsel. Examined by Mr. Cayley:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I will be calling you "Witness X" during your testimony. This, as I explained to you, is to protect your identity. A few preliminary questions for you. What is your nationality?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: I am a Bosniak Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you give the Court the dates of your national service in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: I spent a year in the JNA between 1979 and 1980.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you briefly give the Court details of your educational background?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: I started to be a technician, and I have spent my entire working life working with technology as a technician.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to move rapidly ahead in time to 1992. In that year, did you join the Bosnian army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's now move forward to 1994, to August of 1994. What unit of the Bosnian army did you join at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: In August 1994, I joined the unit for electronic surveillance and anti-electronic warfare.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could the usher please place on the ELMO, Madam Registrar, Prosecutor's Exhibit 138.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, were you given any training prior to operational service in this unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: I received training after I joined that unit, that is to say, one month later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How much training did you receive?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: The training lasted a month, and I was taught the basics of radio technology, because I knew nothing in the field. So they taught us the basics of that job.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, if you could move that exhibit down towards the witness about two or three centimetres. No, down. Yes, sorry, towards me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, could you point out on that exhibit, using the pointer, and you need to do it on the copy on the ELMO, the location of this anti-electronic unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: This place here.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So let the record show that the witness is indicating a green circle marked "Okresanica" on Prosecutor's Exhibit 138. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you started work at the unit in August of 1994. Can you explain to the Judges what the purpose of this unit was at Okresanica very briefly, because the Judges have heard from a number of witnesses on the same point.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: I was part of a unit entrusted with the task of monitoring conversations on military frequencies of the enemy Serb side, and we monitored what we referred to as relay links. And if a conversation was interesting to us, then the conversation was taped from the receiving device onto a tape recorder, and then it was taken down on paper from the tape recorder. This paper went to a department, which typed it out and introduced it into the computer and sent it out to the command. So that was my basic task.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you were unable to properly hear a conversation when listening to a tape, what would you do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: There were many difficult situations, that is to say, where we could hear the conversation but that there was a lot of interference and it was partly audible. But where the conversation was clear, the request was that anything we take down in written form should comply with the original. So if everything was clear, we would write it down. If it was inaudible or not clear, we would put three dots, and we did not write anything because we weren't able to understand it sufficiently.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If there was ever an occasion where something was reasonably audible, did you and your colleagues listen to the tape together to decide what the speaker was saying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: We tried to do that. We did our best to understand the incoming information on the tape. There were different ways of doing this. Some of my colleagues had a greater affinity for some of the speakers, others knew the speakers less well. So we would help each other to record every conversation authentically.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you say in your evidence that you would essentially write down from the tape, from the recording on the tape into a written form, and you then explained that that written report was typed and processed and sent out. Could you tell Their Honours a little bit more about the details of that procedure?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: I should just like to correct you and say that the report wasn't processed after it was typed. The report was typed by the soldier who was responsible to me but officially in the command, and then would just send on the report in the same state that I handed it to him. It was not up to him to change anything. He didn't -- he wasn't allowed to change anything, and sometimes we would read the report. A report which would be sent on to the command would go to the command itself and be processed there. I never worked in the command on the processing of reports. And that was the procedure that we followed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To whom was your unit directly subordinated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Our unit was within the composition of the command of the 2nd Corps of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Judges very briefly the shift procedures that were adopted within your unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Our shifts lasted -- that is to say, we had two groups, two groups of soldiers. One worked on the device and the others were resting, and we would take turns. We would hand over our duty to each other. And the commanders of the platoons or the companies would be present when the shifts replaced each other. This was an opportunity for the soldiers to become acquainted with their tasks and assignments for the following shift and receive suggestions from their colleagues working on the previous shift. As this also meant taking over the devices when the shifts changed, (redacted) (redacted) for the time spent in the location in order to perform all the functions; that is to say, we had to cook for ourselves, we had to see to hygiene and things of that kind as well, (redacted).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long were the shift periods?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: The shifts -- the shortest shifts were seven days. Sometimes they would last 15 or more days depending on the circumstances. Sometimes we would all be working together; that is to say, there would be no replacement of shifts but the shifts would work together. Then we would have a rest period after that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whilst you were on shift, for how many hours did you work in a day? Were there shifts within the 7 or 14-day shifts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Usually we would have two groups and we would expand these groups, but there were never less people in the groups, there could only be more, and our command always requested as many people as possible in the room, the actual room where we did our work. (redacted) and work there and align this with their physical capabilities. Sometimes there were too few of us and too many obligations and responsibilities, so we were very taxed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So there were occasions when within the 7 or 14-day period you were unable to take any breaks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Yes, there were occasions like that, especially for the responsible individuals, those who led the shift, because they were, in part, responsible for the order and running of the work and to see that the plan set by the command was put into practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown Prosecutor's Exhibits 298 and 299, please, and if 300 could be prepared, which is a sealed exhibit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you recognise this photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Those are two devices. One device was intended for the monitoring of radio relay connections, and it is the AR800, and the second device was for RRU1 for relay stations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you point to the device and name it? Because I'm not familiar with the devices myself. The device on the left of the photograph on Prosecutor's Exhibit 298, what is that device?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: The device on the left-hand side is an amateur device for short wave radio communication, and it has an addition which adapts it for radio relay, and it is the Kenwood 4500 device. We had two of these. So this is the device on the left-hand side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the device on the right-hand side of this photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: The device on the right-hand side of the photograph is the ICR100 device with a range from 0 to 1,000 megahertz, and it is for monitoring radio relay connections of the RRU1 enemy lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let the record show the witness is pointing on the right-hand side to the larger black box.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you use these pieces of equipment while you served in the unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Yes, we did. We used these pieces of equipment and other similar equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And if 299 could be placed on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And very briefly, Witness, what is this photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: That is a tape recorder of the Uher type. It is intended for recording interesting conversations, that is to say, conversations that could be heard on the receiver devices.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how was it connected to the receiver?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: The Uher tape recorder is connected all the time to the receiver, one of the two receivers that you showed on the previous photograph, and it is switched on manually by the button. As soon as an interesting conversation comes up, it is switched on. I switch it on, as the operator.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If now the witness could be given Prosecutor's Exhibit 300, and do not place this on the ELMO, please, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, could you look at the second name on that list and confirm or otherwise whether that is you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Yes, that is my name and surname.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And that, Your Honours, is Prosecutor's Exhibit 300, which was introduced by the first of the series of witnesses, listing the people who worked at Okresanica in July and August of 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, finally on the process itself, how did you identify the speakers within any conversation that you listened to and that you recorded onto the tape?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: There were many problems in identifying the speaker, but the command's request was reliable information. Very often the speakers, in the conversation or during the conversation itself, they would mention their own names, so that was a way that we heard who the speakers were. Second, having done this work for a long time, we knew the participants in the conversations very well without them having to introduce themselves. If we did not know who the participants in the conversation were, we would place "X" or "Y", the letters "X" or "Y".

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. If the witness could now be shown Prosecutor's Exhibit 319, and that's specifically 319C. And I would suggest that if we put anything on the ELMO, it is the English version, since the Bosnian written version has the signature of the witness. If you could give it to the witness, please, Mr. Usher. Madam Registrar, just so that we're in a position to deal with this, we need all of the notebooks as well, which is 279, 284, 290, and 282.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you recognise 319C?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: I recognise it. I recognise the first paper that has been handed to me. That is some information that I heard and recorded and made a note of and sent to the command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think on the last page of this four-page document, there is, in fact, a typed copy of the conversation.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this an example of the process that was carried out at the unit of one of the soldiers typing into the computer the written version for transmission up the chain of command?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, if the witness could be shown Prosecutor's Exhibit 279.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, previously, Witness, I've shown you some notebooks, and I just wish you to confirm or otherwise -- I will direct the usher to the page so that you don't have to go through the whole file -- whether or not the report that you've just read out is contained within that particular notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, if you could assist the witness, please, it's Prosecutor's Exhibit 279 and the page number in the top right-hand corner is 45. And, Your Honours, the registration number from the Evidence Unit, the last four digits, which are the only four you need, are 8906. I think it's the previous exhibit, Mr. Usher. It's the first exhibit in this book. Mr. President, may I approach the witness, because I think it will probably facilitate matters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, if you could look at the bottom right-hand page that's in front of you at the moment, do you see the conversation at the bottom of that page which starts: "255.850, 0834", and then the word "Urgent" is mentioned. Is that the same conversation that you've just identified in Prosecutor's Exhibit 319 as being a conversation that you took down?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Yes, it is the same conversation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that your signature at the bottom right-hand corner of the page?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Yes. That was how I marked my conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I will read this into the record, Mr. President. Fortunately, it's a very brief conversation. And, Mr. Registrar, the -- if you could leave 279 with the witness, but if I could prepare you for the next one whilst we're doing this, which is Prosecutor's Exhibit 284, which is contained in the same volume. So if you wait one moment I will assist if there are any problems, but let me read this. It starts with the frequency: "255.850. 0834 hours. Urgent." The next line is: "X: Semso Muminovic is asking for V. Pandurevic to call him on number 144 985."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, in this particular example you've use the symbol "X". Is this an example of where you're unable to identify one of the participants in the conversation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in our previous discussions, you had indicated to me that so much time had passed that you were unable to accurately date this conversation. But if you could go to the first -- correction. If you could go to the second and third page of this document. So back to the beginning of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, if we could go back, I think, one more page, Mr. Usher, to the front.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you turn to the next page, which is the second page of the document, 8816. Is there a date on that page, Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Yes, on that page there is a date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the date?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: The date is the 26th of June, 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you turn to the next page? There is a date there. That is page 3 of this document, 8818. What date is on that page?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: On this page the date is the 23rd of June, 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is indicated by the date of 26th June 1995 on the previous page, if you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: The date, the 26th of June, the date at the beginning of the notebook, marks the date when the notebook started to be used.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What does the date on the next page, the 23rd of June, 1995, what does that indicate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: That indicates when the command which gave us the notebooks registered that notebook in its registry book.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, asking you to make no more comment than this: Would it be safe to say that the conversation that you've identified in this notebook was taken down sometime after the 26th of June, 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if you could go to the penultimate page of this document, the last but one.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The last but one page, so that page, Mr. Usher. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There is a date at the top of this page. It has "A/A", which I think is a Latin abbreviation. What is the date on that page?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: The date is the 24th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What does "A/A" stand for?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: It is customary for us to indicate in that way the date when the notebook is placed in the archives.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if the notebook was placed in the archives on the 24th of July, 1995, it's safe to say that the conversation that you took down was taken down sometime before that date?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Yes. When the notebook is filled in, it would remain in the building until the next shift, and when the next shift came, the command would take over the notebooks and place them in the archives.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you use the word "filled in," just to make it absolutely clear for the record, you mean when the notebook was entirely full? When there was no more space left in it to write any more conversations, it would be filed in the archive?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. The whole notebook had to be full for it to be able to be filed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could now be given Prosecutor's Exhibit 320.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just finally on Prosecutor's Exhibit 319, how did you know that the other speaker was Jevdjevic, if you can recall?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: May I correct you? Jevdjevic, yes. I assume that talking to the signalman who established the link, the connection, heard that somebody was looking for something in this particular case. If I had recognised the voice, I would have given the name, but I assumed this conversation was preceded by the signalman of the enemy army establishing communication.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that is missed from the written transcript, because by the time you'd pressed the play button on the tape recorder that part of the conversation had passed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: There were such cases, but the procedure regarding the establishment of the conversation was not recorded as it was always the same.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that as you heard the beginning of the conversation, you would write down the names of the participants on a scrap of paper? Was that your policy, if you heard the speakers identified?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Yes. It was the best situation if you could recognise the speakers.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could now be shown Prosecutor's Exhibit 320/1C, which is the fifth page. It's where you see handwriting, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise the handwriting in this, Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Yes. That is my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this is an intercept which you took down?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If now the witness could be shown Prosecutor's Exhibit 284, and this version that he's just identified can be placed on the ELMO, because there's no signature. For, Mr. Usher, Prosecutor's Exhibit 284, you need to go to page 33, the last two digits of the seven-digit number -- the eight-digit number, if you go to page 33. So that, Your Honours, in that Exhibit 284 is page 00800633. In fact, you can use just the last three digits, because the others are the same throughout.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps the usher should be told that it is separator number 6 in the binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You're absolutely right, Mr. President. That's actually very helpful. The tab number is 6. If you hand it to me, I can -- page 633. If you hand it to me, I can find it very quickly. Mr. Usher, if you could hand the binder to the witness. You can place the other copy which he's just looked at, the extract, on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you look, Witness, at the right-hand column on page 633, is that the same conversation that you've just identified?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I will just confirm that the witness has identified that the extract, Prosecutor's Exhibit 319, is contained in the notebook, Prosecutor's Exhibit 279, and I will just read that into the record. I'm sorry, I've just been corrected. It's Exhibit 320 that the intercept -- Prosecutor's Exhibit 320 is contained in Prosecutor's Exhibit 284. I will read it as follows: "Lieutenant Colonel Popovic asked to be connected with General Krstic at Zlatar /code name/ and as he was not there, he was asked to be connected with the OC, Operations Centre. P: Hello, Lieutenant Colonel Popovic speaking. R: Rasic here, Can I help you? P: Rale! R: Yes? P: I was just up there. R: Yes. P: I was with the boss personally. R: Yes. P: Here where I am ... you know where I am? R: I know. P: Well, you got his interim report. R: All of it. P: It's just like he wrote it ... I was there on the spot and was convinced he had received some numbers ... well, that's not even important ... I'll come there tomorrow, so tell the General ... I've finished the job. R: You finished? P: I finished everything. R: Good. P: I'll come there tomorrow when I'm sure that that's all been taken care of, you know. R: Good. P: After I bring a transport from there. R: Right. P: Well, in general, there weren't any major problems. But up there, there were horrible problems and that thing the commander sent, it was just the right thing. R: Good. P: Just the thing ... horrible ... it was horrible. R: Listen Vujadin. P: What? R: Tell me, did anything arrive there now from Vidoje Blagojevic? P: From Vidoje? R: Today. P: Yes ... You mean manpower? R: Yes, yes ... did anything arrive? Something was supposed to arrive? P: Yes, it arrived ... it's up there ... it's up there but it didn't arrive on time and it wasn't brought in on time. And the others who arrived, did arrive, but they were late and so they weren't brought in on time, and that's why the commander who was here had problems. R: When exactly did Blagojevic's men arrive? P: Fuck it, I don't know exactly, now I can't ... R: I know ... the duty officer /as printed/. P: Maybe the duty officer ... here's the duty officer. R: Let me talk to him. P: Okay. D: Hello. R: Hello! D: Yes, go ahead? R: When did Blagojevic's men arrive? D: From Badem /code name/? R: Yes ... when did they arrive and how many of them arrived? D: I'll call you right back. R: Okay, find out exactly and call me back. D: I will."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, this is an example of where the participants in the conversation introduce themselves on the radio, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I know it's been a long time and I can assist you here because we have an exhibit, but do you recall what Zlatar was the code name for now?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: The code name Zlatar, as far as I know, stood for the command of the Drina Corps in Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember what the code name Badem stood for?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: The code name Badem was linked to Bratunac, but I don't know the level of the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If now we could move to the next exhibit, which is 321. And just to prepare you, Mr. Usher, we're in the same main diary, so it's tab 6, and the page number is 36. So you only need to, in fact, turn one, two pages and you're there. Don't place this on the ELMO because there's a signature on it. It's, again, a very short intercept.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise the handwriting on Prosecutor's Exhibit 321/1C, Witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wait a moment, please. I think there is a problem with the French transcript. The French court reporter is not managing to hear the interpretation. I think the registrar is bringing us a solution. [The registrar and the Trial Chamber confer]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think we're ready now and we can continue. Please, Mr. Cayley, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Yes, I do. It is the same conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So just to confirm for the record that the witness has confirmed that Prosecutor's Exhibit 321/1C is an extract from Prosecutor's Exhibit 284.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, if you could go to the second page of that particular journal.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, if you could help him. If you would go back to the second page. Back to the beginning of the journal and then the second page.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, on this journal there is a date. What is the date on the second page of this journal?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: On the second page of this journal the date is the 14th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you've previously told Their Honours that this is the date on which the first entry was entered into the notebook; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So is it correct to say that the conversation which you've identified in this notebook is a conversation that was taken down sometime after the 14th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I could just briefly read the English version, which is 321/2A into the record. It's a very short conversation. "2153 hours. CH 3. Participants: Palma duty officer - Cerovic. D: It's not closed yet but it's under control. C: OK. D: Bye." Witness, do you recall now, after all this time, what the call sign for Palma was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: The Palma code sign was linked to the location of Zvornik. I assume the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we could now move to the next exhibit which is 322, and the linked notebook with this is 290. The tab number, Mr. Usher, is 12.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, if you turn to 322/1C, which is the third sheet on the extract. Do you have that in front of you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that a conversation which you took down?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Usher, you if you could turn to page 1469. And I can help you here. It's one, two, three, four, five, six, seven pages from the beginning, 69.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, if you look on the left-hand page. Do you see the conversation that you've just stated was your conversation that you took down, bottom left-hand page of 1468?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Yes, that is the conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So for the purposes of the record, the witness has confirmed that Prosecutor's Exhibit 322/1C is contained in the notebook marked Prosecutor's Exhibit 290 at page 00801468.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, if you go to the beginning of this notebook, there is a date on the front of this notebook. What date is written? Can you read it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Yes. That is the date. It is the 16th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be correct to say that the conversation which you've just identified as your own is one that was taken down on or after the 16th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: That conversation should have been on the 16th or immediately after the 16th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Again I will read it into the transcript. It's a fairly brief conversation. "Frequency 255.850 MHz. 1622 hours. Popovic -- Y (inaudible). P: Hello, it's Popovic ... boss ... Everything's OK, that job is done ... everything's OK ... everything's been brought to an end, no problems ... I'm here at the place ... I'm here at the place where I was before, you know ... I'm at the base ... at the base, the base. Can I just take a little break, take a little break, take a shower, and then I'll think again later ... basically, that all gets an A ... an A ... the grade is an A, everything's okay ... that's it, bye, take care. " Then at the end of the conversation there is a note: "French is heard in the background." Now, you made this note at the end. Do you remember making the note about hearing the French language in the background?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: In the background you could hear the French language, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we could move to the next one, which is 323, and it's the same main journal, Mr. Usher, so we can stay with that one. And if you could look at the 323/1C. There's two pages. It's been photocopied onto two pages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise that conversation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: That is the conversation that I made a note of.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 1477, tab 12 of Prosecutor's Exhibit 290. And you should look at that page and, indeed, the next page, Witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the same conversation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: That is the same conversation, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So let the record show that the witness has confirmed that the extract, Prosecutor's Exhibit 323/1C, is contained at tab 12, Prosecutor's Exhibit 290, on pages 00801477 and 00801478 to 79.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, again without repeating the process so we try and save some time, this booklet was commenced on the 16th of July, 1995, so would it be correct to say that the conversation that you've identified was taken down on or after the 16th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think if you go to the end of this conversation, you see a typed version of the original, again to demonstrate what you've said previously about the typing process. Is that the typed transmission copy?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I'll read this into the record. This is Prosecutor's Exhibit 323/1A. "1458 hours, channel 3. X - Y. X: On the last point ... in the last sentence of point 2. Y: Wait till I see ... on the last point. X: No, in the last point of point 2. Y: Okay. X: It says: and line 8, Petkovci - Balkovica - Memici. Y: Yes? X: What's to the right of Petkovci? Y: Petkovci? X: Petkovci. Y: Yes, yes. X: Well, Petkovci ... the front line is not in Petkovci. Y: Well, then, in front of Petkovci. X: Well, give it to me from the map, take it off, God damn it. Y: To tell you the truth, we don't have a map here and this interim report was typed by somebody else. X: Listen, listen. Stay on the line. Y: It says Petkovci, front line Petkovci. X: We need to find a point at the front /line/ to put. Y: But it's the same,... it's the same line as before, it didn't move back at all. X: Okay, I know. Y: Yes, yes. X: Hello! Y: Yes, I hear you, I hear you. X: I can't say on the Petkovci front line if the front line is not in Petkovci, you understand? The front line is not there. Y: We use these features /? as reference points/, which villages are near these ... X: Stay on the line. Can we choose a village (a small one?)? Y: Will Androvici do? X: That's not good... That's our area which is being combed and searched... Well, you understand what I'm asking you? Y: You mean across from Petkovci. X: Okay, /?from now on/ in Petkovci. Y: Yes, Petkovci. X: Good. Y: Well, it does say Petkovci here, so it must have been a mistake on the teleprinter. X: Good, good. That's it. Y: Good." If we could move to number 6 -- there's only seven of these intercepts, so it's not too much longer -- which is Prosecutor's Exhibit 324. So if the witness could be shown 324/1C. And, Mr. Usher, to help you, this is from notebook Prosecutor's Exhibit 284, which is one that we've used already. There is logic, Your Honour, to going backwards and forwards like this. I know it's not easy for the usher, but it will become clear. That's tab 6, and in that we need page 52. While you're looking for that, Mr. Usher:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, if you could look at the extract in front of you, is that your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that is an intercept which you took down?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: For the record, that's Prosecutor's Exhibit 324/1C. Now, in Prosecutor's Exhibit 284, Your Honours, we are going to go to page 652. That's the last three digits of the evidence registration number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you have that page available in front of you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Yes, it's here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you also look at the next page too, because I think the conversation ends on the next page. Is that the same conversation that you've just identified?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So for the purposes of the record, the witness has identified that Prosecutor's Exhibit 324/1C is an extract from the notebook which is Prosecutor's Exhibit 284 at pages 00800652 through to 00800654.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, if you would go to the second page of this document, and it's one that I know we've already looked at, so back to the beginning of the whole notebook. If you look on the second page, you've already explained to Their Honours that this date is the date when the first conversation was taken down. Is it correct to say that the conversation which you've just identified in this book took place at some time on or after the 14th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And I will just read this one into the record. It's actually quite a long one, but nevertheless I'll read it. "Channel 3 at 0812 hours. Colonel Cerovic - Vinko. C: Colonel Cerovic wants to talk to him. : Okay. C: Hello. V: Yes. C: Good morning, Vinko. V: Good morning. C: How are you? V: Well, I'm running around since last night. We (went in?) again. C: Where? V: They are up there at Crni Vrh, over there at Potocani, Planinci, the part towards Baljkovica. C: Uh-huh. You mean the ones who are coming out on this side. Is that right? V: Yes, from there and all of them are rushing over here to us. C: You rushed off first. Rushed off. V: I really did, quite right. Well, yesterday we wiped out a bit more than 20 of them. C: Uh-huh. Uh-huh. V: And this morning we started chasing about 150 of them over there. They are in some kind of encirclement. C: And in which area are they surrounded? V: That's the Planinci-Baljkovica area. C: That means in the areas of Planinci and Baljkovica. V: Yes. C: You are good ... Vinko. V: Yes. C: What's your plan for tomorrow for shift replacement at Trnovo. V: I don't have a shift for Trnovo. C: Well, I know that was the order, that you've sent a report, however, that Eskic has just called me from up there and said that he was yesterday somewhere at your place and that he heard you are doing a shift rotation. V: No. I did a rotation of shift at Nisici. C: I'm telling you, the report he sent - there's not way it can be done ... That's Krstic's order, there are no shift rotations until further notice. V: It would be the best if we transfer our complete Corps to the SRK /Sarajevo-Romanija Corps/. C: Yeah, that would be best. V: No, seriously, I've sent you a report yesterday. You could see what kind of losses we sustained. C: Yes, and I presented that to Krstic and wrote him special /report/ based on your interim and daily reports. V: Yes, that's correct. C: To let him know so he can tell the No. 1 chief up there. I said that, currently, in view of these losses, we can't use the unit outside its area of responsibility. V: Then he can take the brigade off the list of the living. C: Well, if we finish this up there at (Zepa?) V: Yes? C: Then we will, there is Blagoje and the others, and then we'll ... V: Then we can. C: Engage. V: Of course. C: Okay then. Is there anything else new with you? V: Well, nothing special. We are all engaged still, because the battalion, every single one of us is busy. C: Good ... please have your duty officer as usual, because he left. Strbac was here just now. V: Yes. C: He is not interested and he doesn't want to do anything while he is duty officer. V: He is very much interested in all of this. C: I got the same impression. V: He always knows. Two days ago I was in the field, to tell the truth, I was flailing around left and right, but he always had a fair idea of where I was. C: I can't get in touch with the commander. For God's sake man, what do you mean you can't? I told him, get a car and go and look for the commander. V: He couldn't be bothered to live, let alone do anything. C: Okay, Vinko. Good luck and stay in touch. V: Thank you. Take care. C: And if you need something, give us a call here and we'll see what we can do. V: Roger. C: Bye. V: Take care."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Cayley, I understand. Perhaps we could go on and complete this, because I think it's the cross-examination afterwards, is it not? So I think that the next exhibit is shorter. What do you think, Mr. Cayley?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, it is -- the time is being consumed by the reading process, and this is actually a very short exhibit. It will probably take me 30 seconds to read it. So I'll just establish the foundation with the witness. Mr. Usher, we need Prosecutor's Exhibit 325 and 282. 282 is a notebook and is at tab 4, so in the same booklet that we have. So if 325 could be placed in front of the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, if you go to the third page of that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So tab 4, Mr. Usher. And you want page 53 -- page 753. While you're looking for that ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, Prosecutor's Exhibit 325/C, is that your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that's an intercept which you took down?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, if page 753 could be placed in front of the witness. Your Honours, this again, it's Prosecutor's Exhibit 282, and the last three digits of the evidence registration number is 753.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, is that the same conversation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So let the record show that the witness has identified that Prosecutor's Exhibit 325/C is an extract from the notebook which is Prosecutor's Exhibit 282 at page 00781753.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, if you go to the third page of this notebook, so back to the beginning, there's a date on the top left-hand corner of that page. What is the date?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Date is 17th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is on page 00781675. You've previously indicated that that's the date that the command registered the notebook; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: This date was registered by the command in its register, and at the beginning of the notebook is the date when the notebook began to be used.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you look on this one, in fact, Witness, there is no date of when the commencement -- when the notebook commenced to be used, on the previous page. The 17th of July is the only date we have on this one. Using the date of the registration, would it be correct to say that this conversation was taken down on or after the 17th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll read this into the record. It shouldn't take too long. "Channel 5. 2158 hours. Lieutenant Colonel Popovic- Zlatar/code name/OC/operation centre/duty officer Delgadasi/as written/ Lieutenant Colonel Popovic was looking for General Krstic, but the General was at home - telephone number 076/731 967. Since the telephones "in the town were not working - the exchange was out of order" they could not reach Krstic, so Popovic left the following message for him with duty officer Delgadsi: "Tell him that we are at Badem/code name/ ... tell him that we haven't finished the job, we are here." And then the name (redacted) appears on the same sheet.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, that concludes my examination-in-chief, so I can offer the witness for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Cayley. We're now going to have a recess, well deserved, I think, a half-hour break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness X, you're now going to answer questions which I see that Mr. Visnjic is going to put to you. Mr. Visnjic, your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Cross-examined by Mr. Visnjic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness X. During the examination-in-chief by my learned friend the Prosecutor, regarding your education, you stated that you had an engineering education and that you spent your whole working life working in the field of engineering and associating with technicians. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us a little more about your technical education?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: I was mostly engaged in civil engineering works, earth-moving activities, and that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your technical education has nothing in common with the techniques supplied in radio communication; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. During your testimony, you said that in 1994 you were transferred to the unit for electronic surveillance and radio interception; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also said that on that occasion you attended a one-month long course for training purposes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will make a short pause between my questions because of the interpreters. You also told us that during that training course you learnt the basics of radio communications; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During that course, were you familiarised with the procedure for the formation and storage of interception documents?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: That was not the subject of this training course, except as regards the actual capture of conversations and their forwarding. There was some discussion of processing, but that was not part of our regular duties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Also during your examination-in-chief, you said that at the beginning of January 1995 you became (redacted); is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you then attend any special course to become that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any of your superiors at the time brief you in any way regarding the procedure or did anyone give you any instructions about the reporting -- about reporting on intercepted conversations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: (redacted).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your work at Majevica and especially after the time you became (redacted), did you receive from your command written orders regarding electronic interception?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Written orders were not customary. A part of the order would come through the communications system into the computer of my department.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said "a part of the orders." Does that apply to the orders I was referring to, that is, orders on electronic surveillance and interception, consisting of the following elements: for instance, defining the enemy, the person you are intercepting, the party you are intercepting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: We knew who the enemy was. Throughout our stay there, we monitored only one enemy. And we monitored exclusively one zone of activity of the enemy; that is, the activity of enemy communications.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know -- or, rather, let me withdraw that question. In your work, did you coordinate with the other facilities at which the enemy was being monitored?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: I had a superior officer, and I did not enter into any other activities except those that were directly assigned to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Yes. The handing over of duty was done in a collective manner when the shifts are changed in the presence of the shift leaders and the other superior officers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On that occasion when you were handing over duty, was any written document compiled?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: No, no such documents existed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When handing over duty, was any document drawn up regarding responsibility for the equipment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: The routes of surveillance were in the computer, and they were defined and only confirmed when shifts changed. No other documents were written. A simple visual review of the area, the equipment, and the devices was carried out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But no document was compiled; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: No, we didn't draw up any kind of document.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: The general distribution for the whole shift was done, but work on devices was envisaged in such a way that the operators always had at their disposal one set of equipment. So it wasn't important whether an operator would be working with one or other set.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your assessment, were all the men in your shift equally well trained?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: I believe they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the distribution of men within a shift, did you keep some kind of a record from which it was evident who worked when?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: At the beginning of every shift, we had a distribution. We had a school blackboard, and (redacted) would simply write down all the activities on that blackboard. But it was not kept as a permanent record. It would disappear at the end of the shift.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So there are no written documents about it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: There is nothing in writing about that, but it is well known, how the men worked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your work, would some devices fail occasionally?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: There were such situations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Or perhaps it could be broken?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Breakage is not a term that can be used for a fault in such devices.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: faults.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you didn't have any rules about that either?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Rules existed. I can tell them. I can tell you about them, if you wish. The first rule was that we had to abide by the instructions for the handling of such equipment, and if we act in that way, there can be no surprises. Secondly, if a fault occurs which the operator is not able to deal with, it is sent for repair, it is reported to the command, the commander sends a replacement.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: We all started the war or, rather, we joined the army as regular soldiers, and, in fact, for a long period of time we didn't even have ranks or titles. We just had certain people for certain levels of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But we're talking about the period of 1995. That is not the beginning of the war. It was the fourth or third year of the war. At that point in time when you became (redacted) in 1995, that position of (redacted), was it envisaged in the structure of your unit or was it an ad hoc appointment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: At that time, this was considered a position that should be part of the military hierarchy, with adequate support.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that as (redacted), you had certain rights and duties stipulated by certain military rules?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: All rights and duties are well known in the army. Naturally, people who are higher in the chain of command than others have greater rights and duties in proportion to the position they hold.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us now focus on the position of a (redacted) in 1995. Let us leave aside these general stipulations. (redacted), was it regulated by any certain rules of service for your unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: I am not aware that there were any such official written rules or regulations, but there was the rules of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina which we abided by.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware that in the rules of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina such a position of (redacted) was envisaged?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Those rules are lengthy, and I really can't remember. I'm not even sure I had enough time to read through the whole rules.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your previous answer, you told us you abided by those rules. Did you abide by them according to some general knowledge that you had?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: A part to the rules of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina was studied at the course we attended regarding salute in the army, for instance, and all other ordinary things relating to a soldier's life.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "at the course," are you referring to the course you attended in 1994?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your rights as (redacted) and duties, can you tell me, on the basis of what did you determine the scope of your rights and duties?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Our duty was to monitor enemy radio relay communications in the zone in which -- the zone determined by the command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you, but I'm talking about your rights as

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: The command, (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: I don't know which documents you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm referring to the notebooks, the exhibits that are in front of you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: We received the notebooks when we took over the shift from the commander of the unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On that occasion, did you make any record on the takeover of the notebooks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: The notebooks were previously registered in the command, and we didn't have many notebooks with us so that we didn't make any records as the register of the notebooks was kept in the command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that the notebooks were previously registered in the command.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did that registration consist of? How were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: On every notebook given to us, a number was indicated, the registration number, and the date when the notebook was registered in the command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a stamp on those notebooks, a seal, or some other marking?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: I do not remember any other markings. I just know that there was the number and the date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the pages of the notebooks numbered?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: I don't remember that particular detail. I think sometimes there were such notebooks, but I don't know whether all of them had numbers. Everything depended on the scope of activities which would abbreviate the normal procedure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "the scope of activities," you are referring to the number of intercepted conversations, mostly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: The volume of enemy communications depended on the activities of the enemy or on the activities of our army. As a result, the volume of our own activities in surveillance would increase.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, due to the volume of activities, some of these, let me call them administrative activities, would be pushed into the background; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: There was no administration in the strict sense of the word. The main thing was to make sure that our basic activities were conducted in a proper manner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But that also depended on the volume of enemy activities, as you just said; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: The work we did had to be done in a high-quality manner. If the volume of activities were greater, we worked more and we engaged men from another shift.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The volume of enemy activities, would that have some influence on whether the pages were numbered or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: I really can't judge about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me how intensive radio communications were in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: It wasn't particularly intensive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: (redacted). But all these men were well aware of discipline and did their work well, so there was no particular need for this to arise, for our relationships to be brought into question in any way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question was: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: (redacted) (redacted).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A soldier sending out messages and the soldier that typed out the messages, was this one and the same person or were these two different people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: The soldier typing out the messages, that is to say, having communication with the command, would be an individual which would come under KZ procedure, crypto-protection procedure, and would enjoy special treatment. And sometimes on certain occasions, because we might have some organisational difficulties, he would help somebody else in doing what they were doing. But this was very rare. So for the most part, I can say that the soldiers would send the KZ soldier their written texts, and the KZ soldier would then forward this to the command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The soldier working under KZ procedure, was he in your group or somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: No, he was (redacted) for discipline, in disciplinary matters, but as I say, he would perform his duty without any special training.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you would hand the conversation you had listened in to to the soldier working on the crypto-protection procedure, KZ procedure, did you have any way of checking that the document had been transmitted further?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: The soldier taking down the conversation in the notebook would make a note of that, saying that the conversation had gone on to the command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I should like to return to a question that I asked a moment ago. When you say there weren't many communication conversations, how many conversations would there be in a shift?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Well, we didn't have any statistics on this, on the monitoring, but that was just a feeling, when things were busier and when they were less busy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you filled out -- completed a notebook, who took it over? Who took over the notebook?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: The soldier who transcribed the conversation from the tape recorder into the notebook would then give the notebook to the KZ soldier, who would then introduce that information into a computer and transmit it to the command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long does this operation last, in your assessment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: This whole operation lasts for as long as is needed for that kind of information to be taken down from the tape recorder, introduced into the computer, and the rooms were next door. The operator's and the KZ solder's office or room were next door to each other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When questioned, you said that there were not many notebooks. Can you tell us what you mean by "not many"? Could you be specific; give us a number, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Well, I can't give you a number because a lot of time has passed since then for me to be able to recall details like that. We were given as many notebooks as they thought we needed; one, two, three, perhaps more. I really couldn't say. I couldn't tell you the exact number of notebooks. Sometimes we didn't have enough notebooks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you would hand over shift, who would take possession of the notebooks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: The note -- we received the notebooks from the unit leader, commanding officer, and then those completed notebooks would be replaced with new ones, and he would take away the filled-in notebooks and supply us with new ones.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And there were no written documents on this exchange of notebooks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: No, there were no records, no minutes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your examination-in-chief and your testimony, you said that you monitored relay communications.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you also said that they were usually -- this was done with the RRU800 and the RRU1 devices.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were able to monitor this with different equipment, different devices.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Yes. We had two sets of equipment, two sets, and more sets if we needed them. It was standard practice to have two sets. This meant a device to monitor the RRU800 and the RRU1.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what communications you heard better, the RRU800 or the RRU1? Which were better audible, more audible?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Well, this was not determined specifically on the basis of one or other device, it was determined by the location of the device, the quality of the antenna, the weather conditions prevailing, and factors of that kind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the difference between the two devices, the RRU800 and the RRU1?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Well, in principle, yes, I am familiar with the difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to ask the usher now to show the witness Exhibit 284.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Exhibit 284 is a notebook, one of the notebooks that you had occasion to use. Was the notebook marked by the command in the way that you described earlier on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Yes. This notebook does have the markings of the command as I described them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On this notebook, on page 1 -- that is to say, page 2, it has the date of commencement; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: On page 1 is the date when the notebook was put to use.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us make this a little clearer. So the date means the date of the commencement of the first monitored conversation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: More or less, yes. The first date is the first conversation in the notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to ask the usher to show the witness Exhibit 282 now, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May we take it that Exhibit 282 does not have any mark to show the beginning of work, or, rather, the beginning of the first intercepted conversation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Visnjic, we have already seen this. Would you go ahead and ask your question. We already know that this notebook does not have a date. So go ahead with your question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness X, let me ask you a question which relates to -- that is to say, a general question regarding these notebooks. The notebooks shown to you by the Prosecution were in your possession, that is to say, in the possession of your shift during your work in July 1995; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Some of the notebooks, and this was taken note of previously, have numbers -- their pages are numbered; others do not have numbered pages. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Well, I didn't pay attention to details of that kind. I really didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In some notebooks the date of the first conversation is not stated; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Yes, we've seen that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me now, please, did you ever record the day of the last conversation in the notebook?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Well, on occasion I might have put a date. I think that a date should have been recorded, but there was always a date in the computer. So as soon as I received the report, automatically the date goes into the computer. So there wasn't any need for me to write down the date, but sometimes that might have been the case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me, looking at exhibit -- that is to say, the exhibits shown to you by the Prosecutor, 320 and 321, those exhibits and the other conversations that you were shown today, can you tell me whether you are able to determine the exact date when they were intercepted?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: The exact date that you are asking for could be within the frameworks of the date when the notebook was opened and when it was archived, and an assessment of the date itself is a matter of time; that is to say, when the conversation took place and the conversations would follow each other in order, one by one. So you could look at the times of the conversations, when they started, and then you would be able to arrive at the date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you a logical question with respect to Exhibit 282. It doesn't state the beginning or the end. There is no date either at the beginning, that is to say, when the first conversation was intercepted, and on the last page there is no date either when it was filed and sent to the archives.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Well, I don't really understand what you're referring to. I don't know what Exhibit 282 refers to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'll show you the exhibit. It is in tab ... it is notebook 40 or 27. All those numbers are written up on it, and it is Prosecution Exhibit 282. That is how it is referred to in the courtroom. Can you tell me something about that particular notebook? The date of the first intercepted conversation, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: The date of the first conversation could only be a date after the date when the notebook was registered in the command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you received the notebooks, took over the notebooks (redacted) (redacted), did you check to see whether all of them contained this registration number from the command?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: It is difficult to go back in time to that period, but what I can tell you is that most of the notebooks did have that, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you check that yourself? Are you sure of that, or do you leave room for --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: The notebooks were protected in a way. So new notebooks, old notebooks, it was the KZ soldiers who had it, and these soldiers were particularly selected. They were trusted people. And as this is a small number of notebooks. I do believe that most of them had a registration in the command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell me something about Exhibit 282? When do you think the last conversation took place that was recorded in that notebook?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: I really can't remember the contents of that notebook. However, if the date when the notebook was filed and sent to the archives, then the last conversation was before that archive date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you look at the exhibit and tell us if there is an archive date?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: I did not see that date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. The conversations you intercepted were recorded on the Uher tape recorders, were they not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: All monitored conversations that were of interest were taped on the tape recorder, yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Later on, would you hand over the tapes that you recorded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: The tapes were not usually handed on further, transmitted further. There were times when the tapes were sent to the command to be listened to again, but during that particular period of time, probably because we didn't have the necessary material and technical equipment, the tapes from that shift were wiped clean if we failed to get any reserve tapes. So part of the tapes went to the command for the information to be checked out and for the tapes to be listened to again, but it depended.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who decided whether the tapes would be wiped out and retaped, reused?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: The decision came of its own accord. If you didn't have any more tapes to tape the conversations, then you had to use the ones you had again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: I usually asked for new tapes to be sent, and sometimes I would get a new tape, other times I would not. I also had a superior officer in my shift who would take care of matters like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the time span of the matters we're dealing with, and during your testimony, you said on one occasion that you paid particular attention to the route that -- just one moment, please -- the route that the members of the BiH army were to leave the Srebrenica area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: I felt a human responsibility for these people that were withdrawing, and that is why I wanted to do what we were doing in the spirit of assistance. That was my main concern, and I wanted to see that through my information, that the situation could be solved.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have no further questions of this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Visnjic. Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have no further questions for the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Cayley. Judge Fouad Riad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have one simple question for you; perhaps not simple. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You mentioned, during your answer to the Prosecutor, that Popovic had left a message for General Krstic, telling him that, and I quote you, "We have not finished the job, we are here." My question is: Could you detect approximately where the message would be coming from? When he says, "We are here," could you detect where that is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Your Honour, my department duty was to forward information to the department for the processing of information through an encrypted -- to assist them in encryption that we had in the unit. For some links, it is possible, technically, to identify the route or the direction for some of the connections that we surveyed. For others, unfortunately, it is difficult to identify. But, in any event, that was not our duty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness X.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Judge Fouad Riad. Judge Wald.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Witness X, you told us in the beginning that part of your duties as you're listening to the conversations on the radio, that if you found one that was -- I think you used the word -- interesting, you would then manually put it on the tape, transcribe it on the tape. Did you have any briefings, or who told you, in essence, what would be an "interesting" conversation and what would not, since so many of the conversations appear to be in some kind of code? I mean people are using code words all the time. What was your source of information as to the type of conversations that would be "interesting"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: We monitored the enemy radio relay communications and the conversations mainly of military officers, leading officers, using those communications.
