There was no official coding of those conversations, as a rule. These were open-line communications when people simply used different words for what they meant. They wouldn't use the name. They would say "the chief," or something like that. As for the coded communications, they were monitored in a different manner, and they were not transmitted, but they were not the object of our monitoring. They were teleprinter connections and so on. As to how we judged whether a conversation was interesting, the importance of the conversation is something that we were taught at the course. Important people conduct important conversations. So even the classification of the channels on the devices were made appropriately so that if an important headquarters or an important person is heard, we listen in, and if there are no such people, then we listen to what we have. It depends on whether there's any interest in a conversation or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: During the period that we're talking about, roughly July of 1995, when you, I believe, said that the radio communications were not particularly intensive -- I think you said that -- could you give me a rough estimate, very rough, of, in your own experience, how many of the conversations that you heard would be transcribed; just like a few, many, or almost all? In other words, of all the conversations that came over on the tape, how many you would punch the manual lever and have transcribed. A majority, a few, or almost all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: In my judgement, most of the conversations that were listened in to, precisely because of the poorer intensity of communications, were transcribed because that was all we had to offer the command as information. But when I say "low-intensity communication", I wanted to say that in some situations, both shifts would be working who could hardly manage to transcribe all the conversations throughout their working hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. I have one last question. Take, for example, Exhibit 324, which is a conversation that you identified between Colonel Cerovic and Vinko. I don't know if you have that in front of you. It's 324. I'm only interested in the procedures here, not in the substance of the conversation. It says at the top: "Colonel Cerovic to Vinko." Now, you just said that one of your criteria for transcribing was important people and certain headquarters. Now, this whole conversation is -- at least the copy we have -- is only in terms of Colonel Cerovic and Vinko, and it starts out: "Colonel Cerovic wants to talk to him." "Okay." And it goes down all the way down calling him "Vinko". But it's quite apparent from the excerpt that Vinko is a person of some importance in terms of some kind of command and authority. In a situation like that, does it mean that Vinko never identified his last name, or that you didn't recognise who it was, or that you tuned into the conversation maybe a second too late or something and didn't get it? Because it would appear it would be easy for somebody who monitored a lot of conversations to figure out who Vinko was. I just wondered what your routine was. If you had a first name like that and a pretty good idea of the person's position, would any attempt be made to try and find out who he was or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: I have already said that we had a department for the processing of information, and we could only suggest to that department that an individual whose voice we had heard, we couldn't put a note saying that we had identified him. But the report here shows that this is the third channel of the radio relay device, which means that it was rated very high. We see that the speakers have high ranks in the army. What could happen, and what happened very often, was for us not to start transcribing the conversation from the very beginning, which means we hear the telephone ring, we hear this on the device, and then the signalman of that location answers. And the conversation starts with greetings, questions like, "Who is calling, why," and then the person calling would give his name or not, ask for someone by rank or by name. As I cannot remember everything, I would say that Mr. Cerovic introduced himself and that all he said was that he wanted to speak to Vinko. And that was probably what preceded the conversation before this. However, as this conversation was complete, only this procedure of establishing a connection was not noted down because it would be a waste of time for the operator.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: So your assumption on something like this is when you sent it up, the transcribed version, when you sent it up to your command forces, that they would be able to figure out who Vinko was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: In this situation such as we have here, that is not a problem, not even for the soldier who received or captured the message. But it is the command who did all that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: It's not a problem for me either. I just wondered what the procedure was. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Judge Wald. Could the usher go to the witness. I would need his assistance. Mr. Usher, could you show the witness Exhibit 279, page 3. It is tab 1. So the third page of the document and page 1 of the notebook. Witness X, you have this code of registration in the command, according to what you explained to us. Could you decode for us what is written here? What does it mean? You see the date, the 23rd of June, 1995. And then the next line, what does that line say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: The date is the date on which the notebook was registered in the command on the 23rd of June, 1995. So as this report doesn't have a date, it was compiled after the date when the notebook was registered in the command. The first report has the time when it was compiled and the frequency from which the conversation was captured.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What does "Strogo Pov" mean? "08/2/01/443", what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: I only know about the Strogo Pov. It is the level of confidentiality of the document. It means it is not accessible to anyone except to people within our unit, in my opinion, and those superior to us. As for the other numbers, except for the date, I don't know what they signify. They are numbers from the command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me put the question in a different manner. The notebooks, were they numbered according to any kind of sequence or order?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: I believe they were, though I didn't pay any particular attention to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another question. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: (redacted) sometimes the shift would be reinforced by another shift, and sometimes we were joined by people from headquarters. So up to 15 men engaged on these activities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you remember what age they were, more or less?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: They were mostly -- (redacted) (redacted), I would say, about 25, not more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: (redacted) (redacted).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I think that we have no more questions for you. You have helped us to understand these procedures a little better. So we wish to thank you very much for coming here, and we wish you a safe journey to your country and success in your work. Please don't move, because we have some little things to deal with first. I think, Mr. Cayley, we're rather in the same situation in accordance with the ruling of the Chamber as regards admission into evidence. We have 319A to 325, don't we, as exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We are in exactly the same position as we were yesterday in respect to these exhibits. Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: My learned friend Mr. Harmon has pointed out to me that at this stage he would like those exhibits identified which should remain under seal because they have signatures, and I can do that because I actually noted on these exhibits the ones that should not be shown on the ELMO. 319 should remain under seal when it's admitted into evidence. That has the witness' signature upon the B/C/S version. Exhibit 320 has no visible signature on it. Exhibit 321 should remain under seal in the B/C/S version because that has a signature upon it. Exhibit 322 has no visible signature, so it can remain a public document. Exhibit 323, again, has no signature on it so it can remain a public document, and I think the same is true for Exhibit 324. No, I'm sorry. That has a signature on it. Exhibit 324 should remain under seal in the B/C/S version, and also 325 because that has a name upon it which could identify somebody involved in the process. So that should also remain under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Cayley. Mr. Visnjic or Mr. Petrusic, regarding the admission of exhibits, those of today and, generally speaking, do you already have an idea as to when you will be able to take a final position regarding admission of these tendered documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, sometime at the beginning of next week we will be able to take a position on some documents except for the last batch. We are having some difficulty with the translation. I can tell you that that is the greatest problem we're having, regarding the precision of translations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, Madam Registrar, please take note of these indications so that we can make a ruling. So I think the time has come for a break now. Witness X, please don't move; stay in your seat. We're going to have a half-hour break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see that it's Mr. McCloskey whose going to speak on behalf of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Good afternoon. Good afternoon, everyone. I'm sorry I have not been in the Court. I've been preparing for next week's presentation so we can make it as efficient as possible. On that same subject, Defence counsel and the Prosecution team have been discussing an issue regarding the witness who would be Mr. Richard Butler, the intelligence analyst who would be discussing the some 200 exhibits related to military responsibility in the case. The question I need to bring up with the Court today -- we have been attempting to reach an agreement on what is not a huge subject but is a sensitive subject, and we have been unable to reach an agreement, and so both sides have requested that we -- that we speak to the Court about that now. We would prefer to go in closed session, if that's possible. I look around and it seems like it's closed session at the moment, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps before making the solemn declaration the blinds should be raised. Witness, please sit down for a moment. Witness, please stand up now and read the solemn declaration given to you by the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you comfortable?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're going to look at this piece of paper with your name written on it, and tell us, please, yes or no whether that is your name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So now you're going to answer questions put to you by Mr. Cayley, who is on your right. Thank you very much. Mr. Cayley, your witness. You may begin.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Examined by Mr. Cayley:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you heard some discussion as you were coming in about closed session. Just to reassure you, the visual image of you is distorted and you will be known by a pseudonym. So the public are not aware of your identity; you're safe.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, what is the pseudonym for this witness?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Pseudonym "Y".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness Y, what is your nationality?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Y
utterances.text: My nationality is Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You come from Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Y
utterances.text: Yes. I'm a citizen of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you just give the Judges a very brief summary of your educational background?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Y
utterances.text: I graduated from secondary school. I have secondary education.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How old were you when you graduated from secondary school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Y
utterances.text: I was 18 years old.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you carried out your military service in the JNA in 1998. I'm sorry. Correction, in 1988. Can you explain to Their Honours what your specialisation was within the JNA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Y
utterances.text: I joined the JNA to do my military service of one year in 1988 in the Yugoslav People's Army. I was in the signals branch. I worked as an operator on communications equipment for a time. After completing training that was envisaged for all conscripts, all soldiers, I worked on signals equipment for the needs of the armoured brigade in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was your precise responsibility within the armoured brigade at Pristina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Y
utterances.text: In the armoured brigade in Pristina, after serving for six months, I was a squad leader on armoured communications vehicles. These are vehicles intended for the command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've already said that you had a signals background in the JNA. Were you responsible for the communications equipment within those communications vehicles?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Y
utterances.text: Yes, I was responsible for communications equipment. We mostly trained ourselves, because these were Russian-made communications equipment, on the basis of textbooks. We had textbooks to study.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to joining the JNA did you have an interest in radio communications?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Y
utterances.text: Yes. Before I went to do my military service, I was a radio amateur, ever since 1984. I passed a radio amateur classification test for Category C, and I had used communications equipment before, and it was the reason why I was deployed in that branch of the army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the Category C licence is an internationally recognised radio licence, is it not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Y
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to move forward now to July of 1992. I think at this time you joined a particular unit of the Bosnian army. Could you tell Their Honours what unit that was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Y
utterances.text: It was a unit for electronic surveillance and anti-electronic warfare.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I know that that unit was based in a number of different places, but where was the eventual location of that particular unit? What was the name of the place where it was ultimately based?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Y
utterances.text: We were first near my town for a while and then we moved to Okresanica, and we had another section in Konjuh.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to concentrate on Okresanica first.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown Prosecutor's Exhibit 138, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While we're waiting for that exhibit, to whom was the unit at Okresanica answerable to? Who was your superior command?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Y
utterances.text: The company commander was in the headquarters of the 2nd Corps. So they were responsible. We at Okresanica were accountable to the company commander, and he was situated in the corps command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that was the 2nd Corps of the Bosnian army based in Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Y
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you just point to the Judges the location Okresanica where you were based?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Y
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let the record show the witness has identified Okresanica on Prosecutor's Exhibit 138 as his location, and also the second location, Konjuh, that we'll come to in a moment, as another place where he himself was based.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, very briefly because the Judges have heard this procedure a number of times, can you explain to Their Honours the reason why you were at Okresanica, what you were doing there, and how you went about the process, the function that you were carrying out there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Y
utterances.text: At Okresanica, which is a high hill, a high mountain, and we were located there in order to be able to monitor communications, specifically radio relay communications. We had a working premises in which the devices were set up. The procedure was that at every work post there was a tape recorder -- it was usually an Uher in terms of make -- then two devices for each work post, two devices. I usually also had an ordinary piece of paper in front of me. The device already had memorised frequencies that we were monitoring, the channels, so that I would switch on the device and it would search, do the searching. When a conversation was detected, we would stop the scanning process and we would switch on the tape recorder for recording. On the piece of paper, I would usually note down the time, the frequency, and if I knew the participants, then also the participants. If I did not know who the participants in the conversation were, then a part of the conversation that would be indicative and the number shown on the tape recorder to indicate which part of the tape the conversation was recorded on, and at the end of the conversation, we would usually let the device scan those same frequencies because the conversation may, in the meantime, appear on a different channel. What happened often is that we would record several conversations in sequence, and the procedure would always be the same. We would take down the time, the frequency, and the participants, and after a certain amount of time, if there were one, two, three, or more conversations, we would rewind the tape to the beginning of the first conversation. We would take a notebook in which we usually transcribed those conversations. We would again take note of the time, the frequency, and the participants, and the conversation as it went. After that, when all the conversations had been taken down or transcribed from the tape, we would give them to a man whose duty it was to type out the text into the computer, on the computer. He would do that. He would usually also note the date, the time, and all the other information that we had noted down. After that, he would encrypt the telegram and forward it to the command, the command of our unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the usher could take Exhibits 298 and 299. I just have a couple of questions to clarify what you've just stated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whose conversations were you recording? Who were you listening to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Y
utterances.text: We call them enemy communications. It was the enemy side, the opposing side. These were usually communications between the brigades and the corps and between the corps and the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which army are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Y
utterances.text: The army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you listened to the tape, the recording of the conversation, if you had a problem in understanding a particular word, what would you do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Y
utterances.text: Usually, we were not alone in that room. There were two of us or more operators. I would call -- having rewound the tape several times back and forth to try and decipher the word or the sentence that I can't decipher immediately, I would ask my colleague to help me and to try and hear it for me. If he could not, then we would usually put three dots. If those three dots are at the beginning of the conversation, that would usually mean that the conversation was not taped from the very beginning. That they had already said something, and then we reached the frequency on which they were communicating.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you always able to identify the participants in conversations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Y
utterances.text: Not always. But after monitoring for some time, we already recognised the voices of quite a number of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were the principal manners in which you did identify the speakers in conversations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Y
utterances.text: Each one of us has a different tone of voice, and some have quite specific ways of speech. Some also had telephones that had very strong microphones, so they would distort the voice, and so those telephone lines could be distinguished from others, so we knew which telephone was being used.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And am I right in saying that on a number of occasions, participants actually introduced themselves within the conversation, they gave their name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Y
utterances.text: Yes. When contacting the exchanges, the telephone exchanges that they used, they would often introduce themselves, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just look at the equipment on the ELMO. Is that an example of the equipment that you used at Okresanica or at Konjuh?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Y
utterances.text: Yes. That is a Kenwood short-wave receiver, short waves. And this is an Icon R100, an ultra-high-frequency device.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so in that particular exhibit, 298, there is a short-wave receiver on the left-hand side of the photograph and an ultra-high-frequency receiver on the right-hand side of the photograph; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Y
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And if the witness could be shown Prosecutor's Exhibit 299.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this an example of the tape recorder, the Uher tape recorder that you used at both Okresanica and Konjuh?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Y
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it is a tape recorder. A Uher -- of German manufacture.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this tape recorder was simply connected by cable to the receivers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Y
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It was possible to connect them to headphones. There were connections behind the receiver, and these were connected to the tape recorder, the Uher.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, very briefly, if you could explain to Their Honours, how many days of work did you do and how many days' rest did you take? Was there a shift procedure for your work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Y
utterances.text: Yes. We worked depending on the situation. I worked in several places sometimes seven days, ten days, or fourteen days. It all depended on the situation, how much fuel we had, because for a time we were surrounded, totally surrounded. The roads were blocked, we had no fuel, and so we would be there for 14 days. And very often we would go on foot on location.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Within each shift, whether it was seven or ten or fourteen days, for how many hours did you work every day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Y
utterances.text: Every day, a minimum of eight hours; sometimes for longer. Sometimes I would work for 12 or even 16 hours. Our service worked round the clock, 24 hours a day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the beginning of every seven, ten, or fourteen-day shift, was there a briefing from the commander of the previous shift to your shift?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Y
utterances.text: During the change of shifts, the company commander would address us, and he would brief us briefly as to what had happened in the previous shift, or the platoon commander; it depended. Sometimes it was the platoon commander who was the shift leader. And they would brief us on the most important developments in the previous seven or ten or fourteen days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And within the shifts themselves, within, you know, your seven- or eight-hour duty, after you took your rest and went back to doing your work, did the intercept operator brief you on anything of importance that had taken place during his shift?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Y
utterances.text: When I came on duty, the operator who was working until then would inform the colleague replacing him on which channels there were any activities and what kind of activities, usually.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I think in May of 1994, you transferred to Konjuh. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Y
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you've already shown the location of that place to the Judges on the map that was shown to you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Y
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the procedures at Konjuh and Okresanica very similar, identical?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Y
utterances.text: Yes, yes. The procedure was, to all intents and purposes, the same.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At Konjuh, could you explain to Their Honours broadly the geographical area that you covered, that you monitored from your location?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Y
utterances.text: Mount Konjuh is a dominant mountain in the area. It is a high mountain in that area of Bosnia. And we covered part of the zone to the left of Zvornik. That is to say, Zvornik was on the left, and on the right was Sarajevo, Eastern Bosnia. We also covered the Ozren area, the Mount Ozren area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you stated earlier in your evidence that you were concerned with monitoring the Bosnian Serb army. Which units or which principal unit of the Bosnian Serb army were you monitoring within this area in Eastern Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Y
utterances.text: We were focusing on the Drina Corps, and in the vicinity was the General Staff of the army of Republika Srpska; Han Pijesak, to be more specific.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In monitoring the Drina Corps, you were also concerned with the subordinate brigades of that corps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Y
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Communications were down towards the corps, and they went one way, one-way radio relay devices.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, previously you have been shown by me the notebooks -- a number of notebooks from Konjuh, and you've identified those notebooks. I would like us to now go through that process in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have the original notebooks, as my learned friend Mr. Harmon did in respect of the first witness on this subject matter. I don't intend to offer these into evidence because they are still part of ongoing investigations. We have made copies. But the witness has only looked at these. He's not actually seen the copies, because when I spoke to him, the copies were not ready. So without wishing to create any confusion, I'd like to show him these documents and then essentially offer the copy as an exhibit to the Court, subject to the limitations that the Court has already placed on those exhibits. And I can undertake to the Court that those exhibits are an accurate photocopy of these books.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Petrusic, do you agree? Do you accept this procedure?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Mr. Cayley, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And I would simply add, Mr. President, if the Defence wish to inspect any of these books, they're welcome to do so. So if I could first of all give you that one, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, could you inspect that book that I've provided to you. Do you recognise that book?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Y
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you just look through it and check that you're absolutely certain that it is a book that you recognise?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Y
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this a book from Konjuh?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Y
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this is Prosecutor's Exhibit 293. How do you know it's a book from Konjuh?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Y
utterances.text: There are parts here which I took down from the equipment. It is my own handwriting. It has a date, the date of the first conversation that was recorded into the notebook, and at that time I was at Konjuh myself. So I was serving during that period at Konjuh.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is the date of the first conversation in that booklet, if you can see it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Y
utterances.text: The date of the first conversation is the 1st of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And for the purposes of the record, the witness is looking at Prosecutor's Exhibit 293, and that date is to be found on 00801875. Mr. Usher, if that book could be returned to me. I'll move to the next book.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, if you could inspect that book in front of you. This is Prosecutor's Exhibit 286. That is the copy is Prosecutor's Exhibit 286.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Y
utterances.text: Yes. This is a notebook from Konjuh as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain to Their Honours why it is a notebook from Konjuh, why you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Y
utterances.text: I recognise this notebook because of my handwriting, and it is the period from the 29th of July -- June, I'm sorry, the 29th of June, 1995, which is when I worked on Konjuh. And there are the participants here that are mentioned, and we monitored this tape from Konjuh alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And the date that the witness is referring to, 29 June 1995, is found in Prosecutor's Exhibit 286 at page 00800823. And, Mr. Usher, if we could move to the next exhibit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could inspect that book, Witness. Witness, do you recognise this book?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Y
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think if you go to the fifth page of this booklet you'll find a date. The sixth page.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Y
utterances.text: Yes, I found the date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the date that you see?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Y
utterances.text: The 21st of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you working --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I apologise, but I don't see the number of the exhibit, not in the transcript. Perhaps Mr. Cayley did mention it, but I can't see it in the LiveNote.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I think you're right, Mr. Visnjic. I think Mr. Cayley is going to tell us the exhibit that corresponds to -- the exhibit number corresponding to this notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Visnjic. It's Prosecutor's Exhibit 289.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you very much, Mr. Visnjic, as well, from me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were working at Konjuh during that period?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Y
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we could move to the next exhibit. The Prosecutor's Exhibit -- the copy, is Exhibit 291.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Y
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise the notebook.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this a notebook from Konjuh?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Y
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the first date that you can see, the first dated conversation that you can see in this book?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Y
utterances.text: The first dated conversation is the 13th of June, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And that can be found in Prosecutor's Exhibit 291 at 00801668. And if we could move to the next exhibit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you recognise this booklet?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Mr. Cayley, but I think -- what is the Exhibit number now?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Prosecutor's Exhibit 281, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you recognise this particular booklet?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Y
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where is this booklet from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Y
utterances.text: This booklet is from Konjuh.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Y
utterances.text: I recognise my own handwriting, the dates -- the date, and that is the date when I worked on Konjuh.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the first dated conversation that you can find in this booklet?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Y
utterances.text: The 21st of June, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And that, for the purposes of the record, can be found in Prosecutor's Exhibit 281 at page 00780291. And the last one is Prosecutor's Exhibit 292. That is the copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The actual exhibit number is 292. It's not as just stated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Witness. Could you look at that particular document? Do you recognise that document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Y
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, one moment. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, could you just show me the front cover of that document? Yes. There's some confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Cayley, perhaps I can be of assistance and give you a break until tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry, Your Honour. You can imagine I feel rather like a juggler at the moment, and a file has ended up here which is not in order. I'll review the transcript, but there is some confusion between the copies and originals, but I will work backwards and get it sorted out by tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
